title: OTP rate limiter uses a global bucket shared by all visitors
business_context: ParcelPigeon's login page lets visitors request a one-time passcode by email (POST /request-otp). Because each passcode costs money and the endpoint could be abused to mail-bomb people, it is rate limited to 3 requests per minute. The limiter runs against the array cache in tests and Redis in production — both implement the same RateLimiter semantics.
user_request: Support got a burst of reports this morning: when one visitor requests several passcodes, EVERYONE on the site gets locked out of requesting passcodes for the rest of the minute. The limit itself (3/min) is intentional and must stay. Find the flaw in how the limit is applied and fix it, and while you're there make sure the fix can't be sidestepped by header trickery.

intentional_defect.summary: RateLimiter::for('otp', fn (Request $r) => Limit::perMinute(3)) never calls ->by(...), so all visitors share one bucket keyed by the empty/anonymous identity.
intentional_defect.root_cause: Without a ->by($key) on the Limit, the throttle middleware's bucket key is constant: the counter is global. The third request from ANY visitor locks out EVERY visitor, and conversely the limit doesn't track identities at all.
intentional_defect.why_it_looks_correct: The limiter is registered, the middleware is attached, and the visible test (three requests then a 429) passes — the limit 'works' from a single visitor's perspective, which is exactly what the visible tests simulate.

non_obvious_invariant: The throttle bucket must be keyed per caller identity (e.g. IP address or destination email), not shared: (1) exhausting the limit as visitor A must not throttle visitor B; (2) the identity must not be client-controlled (a spoofable X-Forwarded-For header must not mint fresh buckets).
expected_diagnosis: The agent must know that Laravel's Limit is global unless keyed with ->by(), and choose a server-controlled identity (request IP, or the validated destination email) — not a client-supplied header.
safe_fix_constraints: The effective limit stays 3 requests per minute per identity.
The route, middleware name, and endpoint contract stay unchanged.
The chosen key must not be forgeable by the client.
failure_explanation: Any visitor's third request within a minute starts failing EVERYONE with 429 for the rest of the minute — an attacker (or one unlucky NAT'd office) trivially denies the whole login flow, while the shared counter means no caller identity is actually tracked.
